newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: OLYMPICS-MENEM CLAIMS CREDIT FOR BUENOS AIRES SELECTION.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-MENEM CLAIMS CREDIT FOR BUENOS AIRES SELECTION.

text.p: Argentina's President Carlos Menem claimed credit for the selection of Buenos Aires on Friday as one of the five final candidates to host the 2004 Summer Olympics.

"This happy development is an achievement of the national government, which launched the project and endorsed it all along," Menem told the state-run Telam news agency soon after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) short-listed Argentina's capital.

The president said the design of a nine-mile by 1.5-mile (14 by two km) "Olympic loop" stretching along the River Plate, where 90 percent of the competitions would take place, "elicited worldwide admiration".

Menem, a keen golfer, soccer player and racing driver, said that last year he held a long chat in Lausanne with IOC chairman Juan Antonio Samaranch in which he detailed all the efforts his administration was making to promote Buenos Aires' nomination.

A spokesman for Coprose, the ad-hoc group set up by the Sports Secretariat to promote Buenos Aires' candidacy, told reporters the city was chosen due to an "impeccable technical report" presented by Argentina.

"Starting tomorrow, and until September, 111 people (from the IOC) will come to oversee what we have promised in the report," Coprose spokesman Roberto Eguia said. "We need to get the vote from 56 of them to be chosen as venue of the Games."

This is the fifth time Buenos Aires is bidding for the Olympic Games, after failing in 1936, 1944, 1956, when it was runner-up, and 1968. Its selection offers South America the chance to stage the Olympics for the first time.

The "Olympic loop" would run alongside downtown Buenos Aires and include the soccer stadiums of arch-rivals Boca Juniors and River Plate, the vast Luna park stadium for boxing and other events, a horse track, a polo field, and the Buenos Aires lawn tennis club.

Water sports would take place on the River Plate, whose mud brown waters look cleaner after the Buenos Aires port was moved away from the heart of the city and replaced with a posh complex of restaurants, offices and a marina.
Buenos Aires, with relatively little street crime for a city of 12 million, is touting itself as a "safe" option.
Coprose members also claim the sport-loving, boisterous city has a relatively low pollution level -- an issue which has been raised in the case of other contestants.
Organisers admit that probably one of the biggest challenges for Buenos Aires, which needs an estimated investment of $550 million, will be the need to boost hotel space by between 50 to 70 percent.
